B02.claim_text: Federal Reserve History records Black Monday on 1987-10-19, when the DJIA fell 22.6% in one session amid a global market crash.
B02.hindsight_warning: The source is retrospective; the crash itself was contemporaneously observable.
B02.allowed_content_use: Use as dated market-stress context between B02 sub-cycles.
B02.forbidden_inference: Do not claim the crash was caused by the Fed path or that later B02 cuts were mechanically determined by this event.

B02.claim_text: Federal Reserve History records the Fed's public readiness to provide liquidity after Black Monday and describes operational efforts to support market functioning.
B02.hindsight_warning: The historical essay was written later, although the liquidity statement was public on 1987-10-20.
B02.allowed_content_use: Use to explain the financial-stability response surrounding the 1987 sub-cycle.
B02.forbidden_inference: Do not equate liquidity support with a validated asset-bottom signal.

B02.claim_text: Federal Reserve History notes that the 1987 stock-market crash was not followed by an economic recession; NBER chronology places the next U.S. business-cycle peak in July 1990.
B02.source_title: Stock Market Crash of 1987; Business Cycle Dating
B02.hindsight_warning: Recession classification is retrospective and must not be presented as a real-time signal available during B02.
B02.allowed_content_use: Use to distinguish severe market stress from an automatically coincident recession.
B02.forbidden_inference: Do not generalize that a crash never leads to recession or that B02 predicts future cycles.

B03.claim_text: The July 1995 FOMC statement said inflationary pressures had receded after the tightening initiated in early 1994 and announced a modest easing; the federal funds rate declined 25 bp from about 6% to about 5.75%.
B03.source_title: FOMC Meeting Transcript, July 5-6 1995 (contains released statement text)
B03.hindsight_warning: The transcript itself was released later, but the quoted policy statement was released at the event.
B03.allowed_content_use: Use as the Fed's stated rationale for the first cut in the 1994-95 case.
B03.forbidden_inference: Do not convert the statement into proof that the subsequent asset path was caused by the cut.

B03.claim_text: NBER's current chronology places the U.S. expansion between the March 1991 trough and March 2001 peak, so the 1994-95 case is not dated as an NBER recession episode.
B03.hindsight_warning: Business-cycle dating is retrospective and the absence of an NBER recession label is not a contemporaneous forecast.
B03.allowed_content_use: Use to contrast B03 with recession-associated later cases.
B03.forbidden_inference: Do not label the episode a guaranteed 'soft landing' template for other cycles.

B03.claim_text: The Federal Reserve's historical materials page notes that the FOMC first announced meeting outcomes in February 1994 and in February 1995 formalized immediate public communication of all policy-stance changes.
B03.hindsight_warning: This is retrospective institutional context about the communication regime.
B03.allowed_content_use: Use to explain why 1994-95 is a transition-era communication case.
B03.forbidden_inference: Do not compare statement wording across eras without accounting for communication-regime changes.

B04.claim_text: Federal Reserve records describe the January 3, 2001 intermeeting 50 bp cut as occurring amid weakening sales and production, lower consumer confidence, tight conditions in parts of financial markets, and high energy prices weighing on purchasing power.
B04.source_title: Monetary Policy Report to the Congress, February 2001
B04.hindsight_warning: The report was published shortly after the action and summarizes contemporaneous conditions; later recession dating was not yet known.
B04.allowed_content_use: Use as contemporaneous policy/economic context for the 2001 first cut.
B04.forbidden_inference: Do not say the January cut was taken because an NBER recession had already been officially identified.

B04.claim_text: NBER later dated the 2001 recession from the March 2001 peak to the November 2001 trough; the March peak was announced on 2001-11-26.
B04.source_title: Business Cycle Dating Procedure: Frequently Asked Questions
B04.hindsight_warning: At the January 3 first cut, the later March recession peak and its NBER classification were not known.
B04.allowed_content_use: Use to show the difference between first-cut timing and later official recession dating.
B04.forbidden_inference: Do not back-project the later NBER label into January 2001 information.

B04.claim_text: Federal Reserve History describes the September 11 attacks as a major shock that created massive dislocations in U.S. financial markets and prompted a broad Federal Reserve liquidity response.
B04.source_title: The Federal Reserve's Response to the September 11 Terrorist Attacks
B04.hindsight_warning: September 11 occurred more than eight months after the January first cut and cannot be part of the cut's original rationale.
B04.allowed_content_use: Use to explain why the 12-month post-cut path contains a large later exogenous shock.
B04.forbidden_inference: Do not imply the January 2001 cut anticipated September 11.

B05.claim_text: The September 18, 2007 FOMC statement cut the federal funds target 50 bp to 4.75% and said tighter credit conditions could intensify the housing correction and restrain growth more generally.
B05.hindsight_warning: This is contemporaneous stated policy context, not a later causal decomposition.
B05.allowed_content_use: Use as the Fed's stated risk context at the 2007 first cut.
B05.forbidden_inference: Do not say the Fed already knew the full scale of the later financial crisis.

B05.claim_text: Federal Reserve History documents that subprime-mortgage stress was already visible in 2007, including New Century's April bankruptcy, mortgage-security downgrades, lender closures and tightening mortgage credit.
B05.hindsight_warning: The synthesis is retrospective; individual stress events were observable at the time but their eventual systemic scale was not fully known.
B05.allowed_content_use: Use to establish that housing/credit stress predated the September first cut.
B05.forbidden_inference: Do not claim all subsequent crisis outcomes were foreseeable in September 2007.

B05.claim_text: NBER later dated the Great Recession from a December 2007 peak to a June 2009 trough; the December 2007 peak was announced only on 2008-12-01.
B05.source_title: Business Cycle Dating Procedure: Frequently Asked Questions
B05.hindsight_warning: The recession start was retrospectively dated after the September 2007 cut; the official peak determination came about a year later.
B05.allowed_content_use: Use to separate contemporaneous credit stress from later recession classification.
B05.forbidden_inference: Do not state that an officially identified recession already existed at the September 2007 decision date.

B06.claim_text: The July 31, 2019 FOMC statement said the labor market remained strong and activity was rising moderately, while global developments and muted inflation pressures motivated a 25 bp reduction to a 2.00-2.25% target range.
B06.hindsight_warning: This records the Committee's stated contemporaneous rationale and should not be rewritten using later pandemic information.
B06.allowed_content_use: Use as the first-cut rationale for the 2019 case.
B06.forbidden_inference: Do not say the July 2019 cut was a response to COVID-19.

B06.claim_text: NBER determined that the expansion peaked in February 2020 and that the recession trough occurred in April 2020; the peak determination was announced on 2020-06-08.
B06.source_title: Business Cycle Dating Committee Announcement June 8 2020; July 19 2021
B06.hindsight_warning: The recession began months after the July 2019 first cut and was dated retrospectively.
B06.allowed_content_use: Use to distinguish the 2019 easing cycle from the later 2020 recession.
B06.forbidden_inference: Do not treat the February 2020 recession date as information available in July 2019.

B06.claim_text: In March 2020 the Federal Reserve explicitly said the coronavirus outbreak had disrupted economic activity and financial conditions and posed sharply increased downside risks, leading to emergency easing to the effective lower bound.
B06.hindsight_warning: COVID-19 was a later shock and must not be inserted into the July 2019 first-cut rationale.
B06.allowed_content_use: Use to explain why the 12-month post-July-2019 market path includes a qualitatively new shock.
B06.forbidden_inference: Do not imply the 2019 cut anticipated the pandemic.

B07.claim_text: The September 18, 2024 FOMC statement said activity remained solid, job gains had slowed, unemployment had risen but remained low, inflation had made further progress, and risks to employment and inflation were judged roughly balanced; the target range was lowered 50 bp.
B07.hindsight_warning: This is the Committee's stated contemporaneous rationale, not a guarantee of a soft landing or future asset returns.
B07.allowed_content_use: Use as the 2024 first-cut policy context.
B07.forbidden_inference: Do not label the decision as proof that recession risk had disappeared.

B07.claim_text: On the NBER Business Cycle Dating page audited on 2026-09-25, the most recent recognized U.S. business-cycle peak remains February 2020.
B07.hindsight_warning: NBER dating is deliberately retrospective and absence of a newer dated peak is not a real-time recession forecast.
B07.allowed_content_use: Use only to report the current official chronology status as of the audit date.
B07.forbidden_inference: Do not convert absence of a new NBER peak into a claim that recession is impossible or cannot later be dated.

B07.claim_text: September 2024 FOMC minutes report that most participants saw downside risks to employment as having increased while upside inflation risks had diminished, contributing to a roughly balanced dual-mandate risk assessment.
B07.hindsight_warning: Minutes provide contemporaneous-meeting reasoning but were released after the meeting.
B07.allowed_content_use: Use to explain the risk-management framing behind the 2024 cut.
B07.forbidden_inference: Do not portray a balanced-risk assessment as an asset-market timing signal.
